# १३ सुखविहारपरिवर्तः । <gloss>13. Chapter on Peaceful Practices</gloss>

->१३ सुखविहारपरिवर्तः ।<-

<margin>K 275</margin>
N 180
W 235
Then, the Bodhisattva-Mahasattva <note>original: "kumārabhūta", often translated as Prince or Youth, here referring to Manjushri</note> Manjushri asked the Lord: "O Lord, it is difficult, truly difficult, for these Bodhisattvas-Mahasattvas to endure what they have for the sake of reverence for the Lord. O Lord, how should these Bodhisattvas-Mahasattvas preach this Dharma-discourse <note>original: "dharmaparyāya"</note> in the final age, in the final time?" 

When this was said, the Lord replied to the youth Manjushri: "Manjushri, a Bodhisattva-Mahasattva should preach this Dharma-discourse in the final age, in the final time, by being established in four dharmas. In which four? Here, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva-Mahasattva should preach this Dharma-discourse in the final age, in the final time, by being established in proper conduct and proper associations <note>original: "ācāragocara"</note>. And how, Manjushri, is a Bodhisattva-Mahasattva established in proper conduct and proper associations? 

When, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva-Mahasattva is patient, disciplined, having reached the stage of the disciplined, with a mind not afraid or terrified, and free from jealousy; when, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva-Mahasattva does not linger on any dharma, but views the true nature <note>original: "svalakṣaṇa"</note> of all phenomena as it really is. This lack of attachment and lack of conceptualization in these dharmas, Manjushri, is called the conduct of the Bodhisattva-Mahasattva. And what, Manjushri, is the association of the Bodhisattva-Mahasattva?

<margin>K 276</margin>
W 236
When, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva-Mahasattva does not associate with, serve, wait upon, or approach kings, princes, high royal officials, or men of the king. He does not associate with, serve, or wait upon other sectarians, wandering ascetics, mendicants, or Jains <note>original: "nirgrantha"</note>. He does not associate with or wait upon those who are devoted to poetry and secular sciences, nor does he associate with, serve, or wait upon those who hold the mantras of the Materialists <note>original: "lokāyata"</note> or the Materialists themselves, and he does not engage in conversation with them. He does not associate with outcastes <note>original: "caṇḍāla"</note>, those who practice violent sports, butchers, poultry farmers, hunters, 

<margin>N 181</margin>
meat-sellers, actors, dancers, acrobats, or wrestlers. He does not approach other places of amusement for people, and he does not engage in conversation with them. If he approaches them on occasion to preach the Dharma, he does so without relying on them. He does not associate with, serve, or wait upon monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen of the Hearer-vehicle <note>original: "śrāvakayāna"</note>, and he does not engage in conversation with them. He does not associate with them in the same place, whether while walking or dwelling. If he approaches them on occasion to preach the Dharma, he does so without relying on them. This, Manjushri, is the association of the Bodhisattva-Mahasattva."

<margin>K 277</margin>
Furthermore, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva-Mahasattva does not preach the Dharma to the community of women <note>original: "mātṛgrāma"</note> by seizing upon any signs of attachment, nor is he habitually desirous of seeing the community of women. He does not approach families; he does not think that a young girl, a maiden, or a young bride is to be spoken to habitually, nor does he offer them polite greetings. He does not preach the Dharma to a eunuch, he does not converse with him, nor does he offer him polite greetings. He does not enter a house alone for the sake of alms, unless he is cultivating the mindfulness of the Tathagata <note>original: "tathāgatānusmṛti"</note>. If, however, he preaches the Dharma to the community of women, he does not do so out of desire for the Dharma <note>original: "dharmasaṃrāga"</note>—

<summary>This passage initiates the thirteenth chapter of the Lotus Sutra, defining the "four peaceful practices" (though here detailing conduct and association) necessary for a Bodhisattva to teach effectively in the degenerate final age.</summary>
<keywords>Manjushri, Bodhisattva, Dharma-discourse, peaceful practices, conduct, association, final age</keywords>
